name: UNK_SparkyCarp
iocPatterns: Alternate data streams used to hide malicious payloads in archives
RAR attachments containing decoy documents and malicious XPS Viewer executable
Embedded reverse shell code in modified XPS Viewer that connects to C2
Exploitation of CVE‑2025‑6218 and CVE‑2025‑8088 via WinRAR
DLL side-loading enabled by manipulating DllPath parameter of RTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS
Use of SSL.com issued certificates for signing malware binaries
Trojanized Rufus installer used as a loader in PipeMagic
Fake ChatGPT desktop application built with Rust, Tauri, and Tokio
DLL hijacking in the Google Chrome update executable
Shellcode execution via Microsoft Help Index File loader
Spearphishing links with personalized email and logo spoofing
Obfuscated JavaScript redirect scripts to spoofed sites
keyCapabilities: Spearphishing with forged emails and RAR attachments
Exploitation of WinRAR CVE‑2025‑6218 and CVE‑2025‑8088 via alternate data streams
Delivery of modified XPS Viewer containing reverse shell code
Directory traversal enabling file write outside intended directory
.NET payloads that download assemblies from a server and execute in memory
Credential theft from Chrome/Edge browsers using MiniBrowse stealer
DLL sideloading into Windows Defender via DllPath manipulation
DLL hijacking of Google Chrome update executable
Use of signed certificates from SSL.com to legitimize malware binaries
Trojanized Rufus loader for PipeMagic deployment
Fake ChatGPT desktop application used as bait
Advanced loaders including Microsoft Help Index File loader that decrypts shellcode before execution
Exploitation of CVE‑2025‑29824 for privilege escalation
Deployment of UpCrypter droppers that install RATs such as PureHV, DCRat and Babylon RAT
Spearphishing links with personalized spoofed voicemail or purchase order pages redirecting to obfuscated JavaScript sites
recommendedActions: Apply WinRAR patches for CVE‑2025‑6218 and CVE‑2025‑8088 as soon as available. Monitor outbound connections for reverse shell activity and file write patterns indicative of directory traversal. Implement application whitelisting and DLL sideloading controls to block unauthorized executable and DLL execution. Verify digital signatures of executables, flagging those signed by untrusted SSL.com certificates. Deploy endpoint protection that detects .NET payloads loaded at runtime, as well as the specific backdoors (SnipBot, RustyClaw, Mythic). Enforce employee phishing‑awareness training focused on spearphishing with forged emails and malicious attachments. Block or scrutinize RAR archive attachments in email traffic. Patch CVE‑2025‑29824 promptly to mitigate privilege escalation exploits. Employ web filtering or DNS sinkholing to block malicious domains and obfuscated JavaScript redirect sites used by droppers. Enable script monitoring to detect JavaScript redirects employed by adversaries.
campaignsText: UNK_SparkyCarp’s known operations concentrate on the Taiwanese semiconductor market, employing an aggressive operational tempo from March to June 2025. The group leverages zero‑day vulnerabilities in WinRAR to expedite initial access and then chains advanced persistence techniques such as DLL hijacking and malicious loaders. Victim types are typically high‑value manufacturers, defense contractors, logistics firms, and other critical infrastructure entities, reflecting a pattern of targeting organizations with substantial intellectual property reserves. The actor consistently uses custom Adversary-in-the-Middle kits to harvest credentials and exfiltrate data silently, indicating an evolution toward more stealthy, long‑lived footholds.
description: UNK_SparkyCarp is a financially‑motivated threat actor that has conducted sophisticated spearphishing campaigns against high‑value Taiwanese semiconductor entities between March and June 2025. The group blends legacy credential theft, zero‑day exploitation of WinRAR, DLL hijacking, and custom Adversary‑in‑the‑Middle (AiTM) phishing kits to gain initial access and deploy remote access tools such as PureHV, DCRat, and Babylon RAT. Their attacks demonstrate a broad toolset that includes credential‑stealing injects into browsers, privilege escalation via CVE‑2025‑29824, and use of signed SSL.com certificates to spoof legitimate software, thereby evading detection in modern endpoint security environments.
goals: The actor’s primary objective appears to be financial gain through the compromise of high‑value semiconductor organizations in Taiwan. Their targeting profile spans a broad industrial spectrum—including manufacturing, defense, logistics, and critical infrastructure—reflecting an intent to infiltrate sectors where intellectual property and supply‑chain data are prized. UNK_SparkyCarp’s campaign strategy emphasizes stealthy initial access via spearphishing, exploitation of recently disclosed vulnerabilities, and the use of legitimate certificates to bypass security controls, thereby maximizing the likelihood of sustained revenue leakage.
